about: Publicly reported 2026–27 men's basketball compensation figures that D1 Hoops uses to calibrate and check its NIL estimates. Every figure is copied from the cited report with its date. Reported figures are themselves mostly unconfirmed: deals are private, many go around the clearinghouse, and agents and schools both have reasons to inflate them. Nothing here is a D1 Hoops estimate.
caveats: Most player figures are reports or estimates by journalists and On3, not confirmed contracts. Schools and players rarely disclose terms.
Some reports give a floor ('at least $3.9 million'), an asking price, or a range. We keep those as floors or ranges and never turn them into a single number.
Reports can disagree (Jackson Shelstad: about $2 million in May, at least $3.9 million in July). Both are kept.
On3's NIL Valuation is On3's own proprietary model, not a reported deal; those rows are marked kind 'on3'.
Program budgets combine revenue sharing and collective/NIL money as the sources describe them; definitions differ between reports.

notes.text: Schools with FBS football were expected to give most of the cap (about 75%) to football, which left roughly $4 million of revenue-share money for men's basketball at a typical power-conference school; collectives and outside NIL make up the rest of a basketball roster budget.

NIL Go (the College Sports Commission clearinghouse) requires D-I athletes to report third-party NIL deals worth $600 or more and asks whether the payer is school-associated, whether the deal has a valid business purpose, and whether the pay is in the range paid to similarly situated athletes. In its first year it approved over $355 million in deals and rejected nearly $90 million.
A staffer quoted in May 2026: 'Everyone over a $5 million payroll is not submitting deals' to the clearinghouse, so reported figures are hard to verify.

EvanMiya estimated the D-I player market rose about 65% from 2025 to 2026 (power-conference players +73%, low- and mid-major players +44%), and that a center costs about 61% more than a point guard of equal talent ($1.3 million vs $813,000).
A poll of 10+ high-major coaches, assistants and GMs (April 2026) put top wings at $2.5–3 million, high-impact guards at $3–4 million and top big men at $4–5 million.

GMs surveyed in March 2026 priced an all-conference high-major player at $2–2.5 million (one said about $3 million) and top stars at $4 million or a little more; one GM expected no more than about 10 players to reach $4 million, an assistant said about 25.
The Athletic (July 25, 2026) reported at least 18 men's college basketball players would make at least $3.9 million in 2026–27.
Wyoming's coach described his 2025–26 split: the best player gets about 20% of the budget, the next 18%, then 16%, and so on down a roster of up to 15.
Industry experts have long warned that headline NIL numbers are often inflated and that 'no one talks numbers'.

cbsTiers.about: CBS Sports (Matt Norlander and Isaac Trotter) placed the 79 power-conference programs plus Gonzaga in seven 2026–27 roster-spending tiers. Average $13.5 million (about $7 million the year before). Conference averages: SEC $17.3M, Big East $13.6M, Big Ten $12.7M, Big 12 $12.6M, ACC $11.9M. Florida, Louisville and Kentucky top $25 million. No high-major spends under $5 million.
